targets.name: C54x common core
targets.description: A device-neutral 16-bit C54x CPU target. This is a semantic and interface boundary, not a claim that every C54x device has identical memory, interrupt, timing, or peripheral behavior.
inclusions: CPU instruction and register foundations that are common across the C54x family and supported by pinned TI evidence
Program-word and data-word architectural concepts needed by the common execution contract
Documented reset effects that can be stated without selecting a silicon profile
Instruction sequencing and status effects only when a requirement has an evidence record
exclusions: XPC and any extended program-page or extended-address semantics
Device-specific ROM, RAM, memory maps, wait states, and boot maps
Exact IFR/IMR interrupt sources, vector tables, and device interrupt wiring
Peripherals, PLL and clock setup, electrical behavior, and silicon errata
Machine-cycle or pipeline timing guarantees until timing evidence and tests are added
VC5402-specific behavior, which belongs to the separate profile target

program_address_carrier.claim: The current public API uses a 32-bit program-word carrier so the common interface does not impose a 16-bit storage limit. The carrier is an implementation boundary only; it does not implement or promise XPC, extended pages, or a device address map.

targets.name: VC5402 profile
targets.description: A later executable profile for VC5402-specific maps, vectors, peripherals, and address extensions, introduced only after the common target is stable and separately evidenced.
exclusions: No VC5402 behavior is implied by the common target before this profile is implemented and tested

evidence.reason: The original assertion overclaimed AR effects; the corrected record narrows the source to its printed field and address-construction statements.

sources.title: Standalone API and architecture contracts
sources.scope: Local project contracts and executable tests. These records are never TI-conformance evidence.

evidence.assertion: The program-control discussion places the current PC value on the program address bus and increments the PC for the next sequential fetch; this establishes the common one-word flow effect without selecting a device memory map.

The program-control register discussion describes the state used to continue sequential program execution; it supports the common sequential PC effect without asserting XPC or an extended-page implementation.

The reset description gives PC=FF80h, IPTR=1FFh, IFR=0, RC=0, ARP=0, ASM=0, AVIS=0, BRAF=0, C16=0, C=1, CLKOFF=0, CMPT=0, CPL=0, DP=0, DROM=0, FRCT=0, HM=0, INTM=1, OVA=0, OVB=0, OVM=0, OVLY=0, SXM=1, TC=1, and XF=1. It discusses XPC only where applicable and that field is excluded from this common target. SP and remaining status bits are not initialized by this reset source, so no value is asserted for them.

ST0 and ST1 are 16-bit status registers. ST0 assigns ARP to bits 15-13, TC to bit 12, C to bit 11, OVA to bit 10, OVB to bit 9, and DP to bits 8-0. ST1 assigns BRAF to bit 15, CPL to bit 14, XF to bit 13, HM to bit 12, INTM to bit 11, reserves bit 10 as read-zero, OVM to bit 9, SXM to bit 8, C16 to bit 7, FRCT to bit 6, CMPT to bit 5, and ASM to bits 4-0; Table 4-1 and Table 4-2 provide the listed reset values.

The status-register description permits ST0 and ST1 to be stored and loaded, permits individual status bits to be set or reset, and describes loading ARP through its documented short-immediate field path. This record does not assert arbitrary data-memory ARP writes, raw status write masks, timing, or reserved-bit semantics.

PMST is a 16-bit processor-mode status register with IPTR in bits 15-7, MP/MC in bit 6, OVLY in bit 5, AVIS in bit 4, DROM in bit 3, CLKOFF in bit 2, SMUL in bit 1, and SST in bit 0. IPTR resets to 1FFh, OVLY, AVIS, DROM, and CLKOFF reset to zero, MP/MC is sampled from the reset pin, and SMUL/SST are not assigned a common reset value on devices where they are unsupported.
The auxiliary-register bank consists of eight 16-bit registers AR0 through AR7 used to generate data-space addresses and as general-purpose registers; this definition does not assign a reset value.
The stack-pointer register SP is a 16-bit register containing the top system-stack address. This register-definition record assigns no reset value.
The common program counter PC is a 16-bit register and Table 6-2 loads FF80h on reset. This record does not establish XPC semantics or any extended program-address behavior.
The single-repeat counter RC is a 16-bit register loaded by repeat instructions. This register-definition record assigns no reset value.

IFR is a memory-mapped interrupt-flag register whose individual interrupt-source meanings vary by device. The common target therefore stores a raw register value without assigning device-specific flag names.

The NOP entry identifies word 0xF495, consumes one program word, has no status-bit effects, and only increments the PC in the common model. Its cycle information is intentionally not adopted as a common-core timing promise.

The direct-addressing discussion defines dma as a 7-bit field; with CPL=0 it concatenates the 9-bit DP field and dma into a 16-bit data-memory word address, while CPL=1 adds positive dma to SP. Direct addressing does not change DP or SP. The source does not specify AR effects or CPL=1 overflow or wrap behavior.
The single-indirect format uses I, MOD, and ARF fields. For CMPT=0, ARF selects the addressed auxiliary register and ARP is not updated by that selection.

The auxiliary-address unit is described as an unsigned 16-bit value and supports premodify ordering where a mode requires it; this record makes no inference about address-domain edges or instruction scheduling.

Table 5-4 defines MOD0 as no modification, MOD1 as decrement after use, MOD2 as increment after use, and MOD3 as increment before use; one-word operands change an auxiliary register by one, and MOD3 is a write-only form.

Table 5-4 defines MOD5 as using the old ARx value for the operand followed by ARx minus AR0, and MOD6 as using the old ARx value followed by ARx plus AR0; this record makes no claim about alias ordering, boundary wrap, or timing.

The indexed-address discussion describes AR0 as an index applied to any other auxiliary register; it does not define selected-AR0 alias ordering, address wrap, circular or bit-reversed behavior, long32 indexed operands, or timing.
The single-indirect description cross-checks postmodify versus premodify order and identifies MOD3 as a write-only form.

Table 5-4 specifies an increment or decrement magnitude of one data word for 16-bit word access and two data words for 32-bit word access. This record intentionally does not restate MOD ordering or the MOD3 write restriction, which remain covered by the existing §5.5.3 and §5.5.3.1 records; it makes no claim about bus selection, cycles, or timing.

The 32-bit data operand is ordered with the first accessed data word as the most-significant word and the second as the least-significant word; an even first address pairs with the next higher word, while an odd first address pairs with the previous lower word. This record makes no claim about bus selection, cycles, or timing.
For CMPT=0, the ARF field selects the auxiliary register, ARP is not updated, and ARP must be zero.
The checked address planner exposes explicit status values and a by-value effect whose rejected-input contract is an all-zero effect. This is a project API contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The P2-W16 project contract requires one declarative X-macro opcode catalog as the only instruction inventory, with macro passes generating opcode identity and metadata, a direct 16-bit first-word decoder, and a function-pointer semantic dispatch table. This is a project structure contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The ti_c54x_cpu_init boundary exposes caller-owned opaque storage, copied bus/config inputs, and a 32-bit program-word address carrier. This is a project API contract, not a claim that TI documents this exact C interface.

The foundation represents unsigned 40-bit values in a defined unsigned carrier and provides bounded mask, sign, and shift helpers without relying on signed overflow or implementation-defined shifts. This is a local implementation contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The current observer tests require per-instance observation masks and compare observer-enabled execution with observer-disabled architectural results. This validates the project diagnostic boundary only; it is not a TI architectural claim.
The versioned registry is the project contract for target, source, evidence, requirement, test, and tombstone identifiers; this is a repository governance claim, not TI conformance evidence.

The private architectural-state API distinguishes OK, UNKNOWN, and INVALID_ARGUMENT, preserves caller outputs on rejected reads, deterministically clears stale storage and knownness on reset, and treats physically zeroed AR/SP storage as non-architectural until an explicit write establishes knownness. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private sequencer application seam borrows a planner result, validates its intrinsic effect shape and requested phase before mutation, distinguishes rejected planner results, unknown and stale auxiliary-register state, and applies at most one checked AR write transactionally. Rejected calls preserve the complete caller-owned state; no arithmetic, bus, memory, timing, or diagnostic behavior is implied. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private architectural-state API exposes checked ARP and CMPT field accessors with explicit valid ranges, knownness-aware reads, output preservation on rejected reads, and cross-field-preserving writes. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private address-effect policy tag is validated explicitly by the sequencer: unknown tags are intrinsic invalid effects, CMPT0/ARP0 preconditions distinguish unknown mode state from mode-state violations, and the generic NONE policy bypasses mode-state checks while retaining transactional rejection. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private data-operand contract owns value-owned canonical WORD16 and LONG32 constructors; zero or unknown widths and noncanonical first/second-word relationships make ti_c54x_data_operand_is_valid return false. The contract does not choose address wrap, bus, or timing behavior. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private sequencer operand-application contract validates a canonical data-operand shape before mode and auxiliary-register state, preserves caller-owned state on rejection, and applies accepted long32 effects transactionally without inferring address wrap, bus, timing, or diagnostic behavior. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private state contract exposes checked DP and CPL field accessors with explicit knownness, width, output-preserving rejection, and field-limited mutation behavior. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private sequencer contract validates tagged direct DP/SP source arms, their canonical field domains, their value-owned operand/source relationship, and their exact CPL policy before reading architectural state. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

evidence.assertion: The private direct-source branches of the shared application seam define deterministic rejection precedence, distinguish unknown mode, unknown source, and stale source statuses, preserve caller-owned state byte-for-byte on rejection, and accept direct effects without an address-register write. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The private direct DP/SP planners return explicit invalid-argument or unresolved-boundary statuses and an all-zero effect for rejected field or endpoint inputs while retaining no caller storage. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The indexed planner returns value-owned effects, rejects malformed fields and selected-AR0 aliasing with explicit statuses, rejects unselected unsigned boundary crossings as unresolved, and returns an all-zero effect for every non-OK result. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The sequencer validates the indexed source arm, canonical WORD16 and POST_ACCESS shape, and CMPT0/ARP0 policy before reading selected ARx then AR0; either dependency produces the generic unknown-source or stale-source status as applicable, and rejection preserves caller-owned state byte-for-byte while success commits at most the selected-AR write. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

Table 5-4 describes MOD12 as ARx plus a 16-bit long offset with ARx unchanged but does not explicitly classify that offset as signed or unsigned; it explicitly defines MOD13 as a signed 16-bit offset added before access, with the sum replacing ARx and supplying the operand address.

The long-offset indirect form carries a 16-bit long offset as part of the instruction and distinguishes addressing with and without an auxiliary-register update; this record does not assert signedness, instruction-fetch sequencing, repeat behavior, or timing.
Instruction class 9B defines a long-word read operand using long-offset indirect addressing; this record establishes operand access shape only and does not assert bus, cycle, or repeat behavior.
Instruction class 13B defines a long-word write operand using long-offset indirect addressing; this record establishes operand access shape only and does not assert bus, cycle, or repeat behavior.

The long-offset planner copies the raw 16-bit extension, sign-extends it explicitly, constructs canonical WORD16 or LONG32 effects with one selected-AR PRE_ACCESS update, rejects invalid fields and unsafe unsigned endpoints, and returns an all-zero effect for every non-OK result. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The sequencer validates the long-offset source arm and intrinsic MOD13 PRE_ACCESS shape before CMPT=0/ARP=0 and selected-AR state checks, preserves caller-owned state on rejection, and commits at most one selected-AR write without redoing offset arithmetic. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

Table 5-4 lists MOD4 *ARx-0B and MOD7 *ARx+0B: the old ARx value supplies the operand address and ARx is updated after access by reverse-carry subtraction or addition using AR0. This record makes no width-scaling or read/write-restriction claim beyond the table text.

The bit-reversed addressing discussion requires AR0=2^(N-1) for an FFT size 2^N, shows reverse-carry propagation from bit 15 (MSB) toward bit 0 (LSB), and provides the worked address sequence 0x60, 0x68, 0x64, 0x6c, 0x62, 0x6a, 0x66, 0x6e with its four-bit table.
Table 5-9 lists the *AR0-0B and *AR0+0B operand syntax as legal forms. This syntax record does not determine update ordering when the selected auxiliary register aliases AR0.

The project reverse-carry primitive has an explicit status and value contract, performs unsigned 16-bit bit-by-bit reverse propagation without signed shifts or implicit wrap selection, and exposes no usable candidate when propagation escapes the 16-bit domain. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The project reverse-carry planner exposes only WORD16 MOD4/MOD7 operands with CMPT=0, selected AR1-AR7, and a nonzero one-hot AR0 value; its validator rejects malformed non-WORD16 effects, invalid fields, non-one-hot AR0, and unresolved boundaries with deterministic statuses and an all-zero effect. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The sequencer reverse-carry transaction validates the tagged source arm and POST_ACCESS relation before ordered selected-AR then AR0 dependency reads, preserves complete state on rejection, and commits at most one selected-AR write without recomputing reverse-carry arithmetic. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

Section 3.3.4.8 defines BK as the 16-bit circular-buffer size register used by the ARAUs to specify the data-block size. This record does not claim circular arithmetic, memory mapping, reset, or timing behavior.
Table 3-3 maps the CPU memory-mapped BK circular-buffer size register to data-memory address 0x19. This is a mapping record only; it does not implement or claim common-core MMR routing.

The circular-addressing discussion defines BK as the circular-buffer size input and describes its relationship to the effective base, end, index, and step for future circular-addressing work. This record does not implement circular arithmetic or select boundary behavior.

Table 5-4 defines MOD8 as using the old ARx value for the operand followed by circular ARx minus one, and MOD10 as using the old ARx value followed by circular ARx plus one; this record covers WORD16 fixed one-word steps only and does not select boundary, LONG32, or timing behavior.

Section 5.5.3.4 defines circular addressing from BK size R: choose N as the smallest integer with 2^N greater than R, align the base to 2^N, derive the effective base and end plus the index from ARx and BK, and apply the step at that index; no adjustment occurs for 0 <= index+step < BK, subtract BK when index+step >= BK, and add BK when index+step < 0. BK=0 disables circular modification, and the first access AR must point inside the buffer. This record does not select unsupported operand forms or timing behavior.

The private BK state seam owns a copied 16-bit value with checked read/write accessors, explicit OK/UNKNOWN/INVALID_ARGUMENT status, output-preserving rejected reads, and knownness established only by a valid write. Reset leaves BK physically zero but architecturally unknown. This is a project contract, not TI reset or circular behavior evidence.

The private sequencer validation seam performs deterministic read-only address-effect validation in its documented dependency order, writes a zeroed commit description on every error, and leaves the sole architectural-state write to the apply boundary. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The circular address planner and intrinsic validator own checked CMPT=0 WORD16 MOD8/MOD10 effects with copied AR/BK source snapshots, strict argument and initial-buffer validation, canonical BK=0 NONE updates, and all-zero effects on rejected planner results. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

The sequencer application contract validates circular effect shape and phase, reads CMPT/ARP before the selected AR and then BK, distinguishes unknown and stale dependencies, commits at most one selected-AR write for positive BK, and leaves canonical BK=0 NONE effects non-mutating. This is a project contract, not TI conformance evidence.

requirements.claim: Implement the reset values explicitly documented for the common architecture: PC=FF80h, IPTR=1FFh, IFR=0, RC=0, ARP=0, ASM=0, AVIS=0, BRAF=0, C16=0, C=1, CLKOFF=0, CMPT=0, CPL=0, DP=0, DROM=0, FRCT=0, HM=0, INTM=1, OVA=0, OVB=0, OVM=0, OVLY=0, SXM=1, TC=1, and XF=1.

Construct private common architectural state with the documented reset seed: 16-bit PC=FF80h, raw IFR=0, RC=0, and the registered ST0, ST1, and PMST reset fields at their documented widths and values; AR0-AR7 and SP carry no reset knownness.

Implement the common status-field layout with ARP in ST0 bits 15-13, DP in ST0 bits 8-0, CPL in ST1 bit 14, and CMPT in ST1 bit 5, plus field-specific writes that change only the targeted architectural field.
SP and remaining status bits are not initialized by the reset source and no value is asserted for them.
Recognize NOP as word 0xF495 with a width of one program word.

The first ISA slice owns one declarative X-macro catalog as the sole instruction inventory; macro passes generate opcode identity and metadata, a direct 16-bit first-word lookup, and a function-pointer semantic dispatch table with explicit unknown-word classification.
NOP produces no opcode-owned architectural or status effects.
A one-word NOP advances the common program counter sequentially by one program word, subject to the common target's explicit address model.
For valid 9-bit DP and 7-bit dma fields with CPL=0, compute the 16-bit data-memory word address formed by concatenating DP:dma.
For valid CPL=0 DP WORD16 and non-overflow CPL=1 SP WORD16 direct forms, direct addressing leaves the DP and SP registers unchanged.

For valid CPL=1 SP16 and 7-bit dma fields whose sum remains within the 16-bit data-word address domain, compute the direct data-memory word address as SP plus zero-extended dma without selecting overflow or wrap behavior.
For valid direct WORD16 addressing, CPL=0 selects the DP:dma source form and CPL=1 selects the SP+dma source form, preserving the corresponding data-word operand address.
Do not choose overflow or wrap behavior at the SP boundary for CPL=1 direct addressing without stronger primary evidence.
For CMPT=0 single-indirect word access, MOD0 (*ARx) uses the current ARx value as the data-word effective address and emits no auxiliary-register update.
For CMPT=0 single-indirect word access, MOD1 and MOD2 use the old ARx value as the data-word effective address and report a one-word post-access decrement or increment respectively.
For CMPT=0 single-indirect word access, MOD3 increments ARx by one before access, uses the new value as the data-word effective address, and accepts writes only.
For CMPT=0 single-indirect planning, an already-decoded ARF index selects AR0-AR7 and is used consistently for the effective address and any update; the planner does not consult ARP.
For planner-produced CMPT=0 single-indirect word effects, require known CMPT=0 and ARP=0 before applying the selected-AR effect; the sequencing seam does not write back ARP.
Unsigned ARAU behavior at the address-domain edges is not selected until primary evidence resolves decrement and increment boundary behavior.

For CMPT=0 single-indirect 32-bit data operands, MOD1, MOD2, and MOD3 use an auxiliary-register delta magnitude of two data words; the direction and pre/post ordering remain the mode-specific behavior already covered by the existing records. Address-domain edge behavior remains unresolved.

Represent a valid 32-bit single-indirect data operand with the first data word as MSW and the second as LSW; an even first data-word address pairs with the next higher address and an odd first address pairs with the previous lower address.

For planner-produced CMPT=0 single-indirect long32 effects, MOD0 uses the first data-word address with no auxiliary-register update; MOD1 and MOD2 use that first address and schedule post-access decrement or increment by two data words; MOD3 is write-only, schedules a pre-access increment by two, and uses the updated first address. Each effect preserves explicit first/MSW and second/LSW operand addresses.

For planner-produced CMPT=0 single-indirect word effects, sequence MOD0 without an auxiliary-register update, MOD1 and MOD2 at post-access, and MOD3 at pre-access while applying the selected AR value documented by the effect.

For CMPT=0 single-indirect WORD16 MOD5 with selected ARx other than AR0, the admitted safe domain uses the old ARx as the data-word effective address and schedules the selected ARx to become ARx minus AR0 after access; subtraction boundary behavior outside that domain remains unresolved.

For CMPT=0 single-indirect WORD16 MOD6 with selected ARx other than AR0, the admitted safe domain uses the old ARx as the data-word effective address and schedules the selected ARx to become ARx plus AR0 after access; addition boundary behavior outside that domain remains unresolved.

For planner-produced CMPT=0 indexed WORD16 effects, the old selected ARx is the operand address, the copied AR0 source is used only for the selected-AR post-access update, and AR0 is not mutated; selected-AR0 aliasing, wrap, and other indexed forms remain outside this slice.

The checked address planner maps invalid enum or index inputs to INVALID_ARGUMENT, MOD3 reads to UNSUPPORTED_ACCESS, deliberately unchosen address edges to UNRESOLVED_BOUNDARY, and returns an all-zero effect for every non-OK result.

The direct DP/SP planners reject malformed fields and unresolved SP endpoints with explicit statuses and return an all-zero effect on every rejection, while copying source fields into value-owned successful effects.

The indexed planner rejects invalid mode, access, and index inputs before alias checks, reports selected-AR0 and unsafe unsigned boundaries explicitly, returns an all-zero effect on every rejection, and copies both source values into successful effects without retaining caller storage.

Indexed application validates the tagged two-source shape and phase before architectural reads, gives mode and intrinsic-shape rejection deterministic precedence, reports the generic unknown-source or stale-source status for either selected-AR or AR0 dependency as applicable, preserves complete state on rejection, and commits at most one selected-AR write without mutating AR0.
The current opaque CPU shell and bus contract remain isolated, caller-owned, and independently testable.
The current 40-bit arithmetic helpers have defined carrier, masking, sign, and shift behavior under strict C11 validation.
The observer seam is optional, instance-owned, and architecturally non-interfering; observation is not an opcode semantic source.
Validate the versioned evidence registry's schema, target/source/evidence/requirement/test cross-references, path states, and exact reverse links in repository quality checks.

Private state reset deterministically clears stale storage and knownness; checked accessors distinguish known and unknown AR/SP values, preserve caller outputs and state on rejected calls, and mark values known only after checked writes.

Checked ARP and CMPT accessors reject null, unknown, and out-of-range inputs without mutating state or caller outputs, preserve unrelated field bits and knownness on valid writes, and expose only their documented field ranges.

Address-effect application validates state-policy tags explicitly, distinguishes UNKNOWN_MODE_STATE from MODE_STATE_VIOLATION, permits generic NONE without mode-state consultation, and rejects every policy failure transactionally without mutation.

The private address-effect application seam rejects null or malformed inputs in deterministic order, never interprets a non-OK planner payload, requires the requested phase and effective-address relation to match the intrinsic effect, distinguishes unknown and stale selected AR state, and leaves the complete state unchanged on every rejection; successful AR effects perform one checked write and NONE effects do not mutate state.

The private data-operand API exposes value-owned canonical WORD16 and LONG32 descriptors with no retained or embedded borrow; its validator temporarily borrows a read-only descriptor, accepts only the defined width and first/second-word relationships, mutates neither caller storage nor the descriptor, and leaves address wrap behavior unselected.

The private sequencer operand-application seam validates canonical operand shape before mode and auxiliary-register state, preserves the complete caller-owned state on every rejection, and applies accepted 32-bit effects transactionally without inferring wrap, bus, timing, or diagnostic behavior.

Checked DP and CPL accessors reject null, unknown, and out-of-range inputs without mutating state or caller outputs, preserve unrelated field bits and knownness on valid writes, and expose only their documented field ranges.
Tagged direct DP/SP source snapshots are value-owned and checked against their canonical field domains, recomputed WORD16 operand, and exact direct CPL policy before architectural state is read.
Direct-source application rejects malformed intrinsic payloads before phase, mode, or source-state checks and rejects non-OK planner results without interpreting their payloads.
Direct-source application distinguishes UNKNOWN_MODE_STATE for unreadable CPL from UNKNOWN_SOURCE for unreadable DP or SP and STALE_SOURCE for a mismatching known DP or SP snapshot.
Every rejected direct-source application preserves the complete caller-owned architectural state byte-for-byte, while accepted direct effects perform no address-register write.

For CMPT=0 MOD13 *+ARx(lk) WORD16 operands, interpret the copied raw lk word as a signed 16-bit offset, add it to selected ARx before access, use the resulting in-range data-word address, and replace ARx with that value.

For CMPT=0 MOD13 *+ARx(lk) LONG32 operands, apply the signed 16-bit offset before access to form the first in-range data-word address and represent the canonical MSW/LSW pair without scaling the offset by operand width.
Planner-produced CMPT=0 MOD13 effects carry the copied raw offset, a canonical WORD16 or LONG32 operand, and one PRE_ACCESS selected-AR update whose resulting address is used by the operand.

The signedness of the MOD12 long-offset carrier remains unresolved: the CPU description identifies a 16-bit long offset but does not explicitly classify it as signed or unsigned, so no MOD12 arithmetic is selected.

The long-offset planner copies its raw extension, performs explicit signed evaluation, validates MOD13 source and operand relations, rejects unsafe unsigned endpoints as unresolved, and returns an all-zero effect for every non-OK result.

Long-offset application validates intrinsic source, operand, and PRE_ACCESS shape before CMPT=0/ARP=0 and selected-AR state reads, reports unknown or stale selected-AR state deterministically, preserves complete state on rejection, and commits at most one selected-AR write.
Implement the common safe-domain 16-bit reverse-carry primitive: nonescaping propagation follows the documented bit direction over the represented word.
For a valid safe-domain WORD16 CMPT=0 MOD4 operand, the old selected AR supplies the operand address and a reverse-carry subtraction using AR0 supplies the post-access selected-AR update.
For a valid safe-domain WORD16 CMPT=0 MOD7 operand, the old selected AR supplies the operand address and a reverse-carry addition using AR0 supplies the post-access selected-AR update.

A valid reverse-carry WORD16 effect preserves the old selected-AR operand address, carries one POST_ACCESS selected-AR update, and retains the CMPT=0/ARP=0 state policy without claiming timing or bus behavior.
Final reverse-carry propagation, endpoint behavior, and 16-bit wrap semantics remain unresolved.
The ordering when selected AR0 aliases the reverse-carry index remains unresolved; legal *AR0±0B syntax does not establish whether the selected value or updated value is observed.
The applicability and update scaling of MOD4/MOD7 for LONG32 operands remain unresolved; no width scaling is inferred from the MOD1–MOD3-only access-width text.
The reverse-carry primitive has deterministic status and output rules, rejects propagation escape without silently wrapping, and remains free of signed-shift or implementation-defined arithmetic.

The reverse-carry planner owns validation and rejection precedence for MOD4/MOD7 WORD16 effects, requires selected AR1–AR7 and nonzero one-hot AR0, and returns an all-zero effect for every non-OK result.

The sequencer reverse-carry application contract validates source shape and ordered dependencies, preserves state byte-for-byte on rejection, and commits at most one selected-AR POST_ACCESS write without recomputing arithmetic.
Represent the documented common circular-buffer size register BK as a 16-bit architectural value without claiming reset behavior, circular arithmetic, or memory-mapped routing.

The private BK accessor contract keeps a copied 16-bit value with explicit OK/UNKNOWN/INVALID_ARGUMENT status, physically zeroes BK representation at reset while leaving its architectural value unknown, preserves rejected read outputs and state, and establishes knownness only through a valid write.
Expose BK at CPU data-memory MMR word address 0x0019 through a future bus/MMR route; state access remains owned by src/state.

CMPT=0 circular MOD8/MOD10 effects obtain a known 16-bit BK size through the state seam and apply the documented R/N/base/index/step algorithm; BK=0 carries the canonical NONE update and leaves the selected address register unmodified, while unsupported forms remain separate requirements.

For CMPT=0 WORD16 circular MOD8/MOD10 forms, admit any selected auxiliary register AR0-AR7, use the pre-access selected AR as the effective address, and produce a post-access circular decrement or increment by one data word respectively; behavior for an initial AR outside the documented buffer remains a separate unresolved requirement.

A valid CMPT=0 WORD16 MOD8/MOD10 effect carries the pre-access selected AR as its effective address and, for positive BK, one POST_ACCESS selected-AR circular update; BK=0 carries the canonical NONE update and leaves architectural state unmodified, while bus, memory, and timing behavior remain outside this slice.

The circular planner validates argument precedence, rejects an initial selected AR outside the documented buffer, copies AR/BK source snapshots, emits canonical BK=0 NONE updates, validates intrinsic effect shape, and returns an all-zero effect for every rejected planner result.

The circular sequencer application validates intrinsic effect shape and phase, orders CMPT/ARP then selected-AR then BK dependency reads, distinguishes unknown and stale sources, commits at most one selected-AR write for positive BK, and preserves the complete state on rejection or BK=0 NONE success.

The behavior for a circular operand whose initial selected AR is outside the buffer remains unresolved; the source requires the first access AR to point inside the buffer, but the project does not yet select rejection, normalization, or other handling.
The circular MOD8/MOD10 update scaling for LONG32 operands remains unresolved; the WORD16 fixed one-word evidence does not select whether access width changes the circular step.
The MOD9/MOD11 circular update semantics using AR0 as a step remain unresolved; no behavior is selected for source ordering, step snapshot, aliasing, or boundary handling.
The signed-offset circular behavior of MOD14 remains unresolved; no signed offset source, premodify ordering, or boundary combination is selected.
CMPT=1 and dual-indirect circular forms remain unresolved; no alternate register-file, operand sequencing, or circular update behavior is selected.

The private address-effect validation seam is read-only and deterministic, enforces the documented dependency and rejection order, zeroes its commit description on every error, and leaves the sole architectural-state write to the apply boundary.
